groups.title: Server Hooks
groups.question: Every page in your SvelteKit app needs to know the current user. Explain how hooks and locals provide this.

followUps.The handle hook and request interception: What does the handle hook do?

evidence.text: handle in hooks.server.ts runs for every server request.
It reads the session cookie and finds the user.
It runs before any load function or action.

notEnough: Only saying hooks run on requests.

evidence.text: locals is an object that lives for one request.
handle stores data like the current user on it.
Load functions and actions read it without looking the user up again.

groups.title: Session and Cookie Concepts
groups.question: You are implementing login with sessions, and the account page must only be visible to signed-in users. Explain sessions and route protection.

followUps.Sessions and HTTP cookies for authentica: How do sessions and cookies keep a user logged in?
followUps.Protecting routes by checking locals in: How would you protect the account page?

evidence.text: The server stores session data.
The browser keeps a cookie with the session id.
On each request the server uses the id to find the session.
The page's load function checks locals.user.
If there is no user, it redirects to login.
The check runs on the server, so it cannot be bypassed in the browser.

notEnough: Only saying you protect the route.

groups.title: Auth Flows
groups.question: You are writing sign-up, login and logout as SvelteKit form actions. Explain how each should work.

followUps.Login and signup form actions with passw: How should signup and login store and check passwords?

evidence.text: Signup hashes the password with bcrypt or a similar slow hash.
Login compares the typed password with the stored hash.
On success, a session is created and its cookie set.
Logout deletes the session on the server.
It expires the cookie in the browser.
It is a server action, not just a client-side change.

notEnough: Only saying logout clears the cookie.

groups.title: Security Practices
groups.question: A security review asks how your app prevents cross-site request forgery and session theft. Explain SvelteKit's protections and cookie flags.

followUps.CSRF protection built into SvelteKit for: How do SvelteKit form actions defend against CSRF?
followUps.Secure and HttpOnly cookie flags explain: What do HttpOnly and Secure cookie flags do?

evidence.text: SvelteKit checks the Origin header of form submissions.
Cross-site form posts are rejected.
Other cross-site mutation paths, like custom endpoints, need their own protection.
HttpOnly stops JavaScript from reading the cookie, which limits XSS damage.
Secure sends the cookie only over HTTPS.
SameSite limits sending the cookie on cross-site requests.
